name: Morgan Stanley
summary: Morgan Stanley's interviews usually mix competency and strengths-based questions with technical questions for the division, and its own interview guidance says interviewers want to see how you work through a scenario, not only whether you get the right answer. Candidates commonly report online assessments (coding tests for technology), a first interview that is often by video, then a final round of several interviews with the team.
rounds: Online application, with online assessments for many roles (coding tests for technology)
First-round interview, often by video (recorded for some roles)
Final round: several interviews with the team, competency-based and technical
looks_for: A clear reason for the industry, the firm and the division
Working through a problem out loud, even without a perfect answer
Knowing your CV and telling your story clearly

questions.text: Tell me about yourself, without looking at your CV.
covers: A clear path through your studies and experience, with the reason for each step
The one or two things you're best at, with evidence
Why this division at Morgan Stanley is the next step

questions.text: Tell me about a time you made an ethical call that wasn't the easy option.
covers: The situation and what made the easy option tempting
How you decided and who you involved
The outcome and what you'd do again

questions.text: Tell me about a time you put a client's or user's interests ahead of your own convenience.
covers: Who they were and what they needed
What it cost you and why you did it anyway
The difference it made for them

questions.text: Tell me about an idea of yours that changed how a team or project worked.
covers: The problem the idea solved
How you got others to try it
What changed, measured if you can

questions.text: What are you particularly good at, and when did it make the biggest difference?
covers: One strength, named plainly
A specific example where it changed the result
How it would help in this role

questions.text: Explain what a wealth manager does for a client, and how the firm earns money from it.
covers: Understanding the client's goals and risk, then planning and investing for them
Ongoing advice: rebalancing, tax-aware choices, planning for life events
How fees work in general terms: a share of assets managed, or charges per service

questions.text: Walk me through a discounted cash flow valuation in plain words.
covers: Forecasting the cash the business will generate
Discounting it back at a rate that reflects risk, plus a value for the years beyond
The assumptions that move the answer most, and a sense check against market multiples

questions.text: If a company issues new shares, what happens to its existing shareholders?
covers: Their ownership share falls (dilution)
Whether value per share falls depends on the price and what the money is used for
Why companies do it anyway: growth, paying down debt, an acquisition

questions.text: Pick one area of the markets you follow. What's happening there now, and why?
covers: A specific, current topic described accurately
The main drivers in plain words
What it means for the firm's clients and what you'd watch next

questions.text: How would you design a system that records every trade and can rebuild any account's position at a past point in time?
covers: Storing trades as an append-only log of events, never overwritten
Rebuilding positions by replaying events, with snapshots to keep it fast
Audit needs: correctness, corrections as new events, and access control

questions.text: A nightly batch job that used to take one hour now takes four. How would you find out why?
covers: What changed: data volume, code releases, infrastructure, other jobs running at once
Timing each step to find the slow one, using logs and metrics
The fix, and monitoring so you hear about it before users do

questions.text: Explain the difference between a stack and a queue, and where you'd use each in a real system.
covers: Stack: last in, first out; queue: first in, first out
Examples: undo history or call stacks; processing orders or messages in arrival order
What happens to performance and fairness if you pick the wrong one

questions.text: Why this industry, why Morgan Stanley, and why this division?
covers: A reason for finance or financial technology, shown by something you've done
Something specific about Morgan Stanley: its businesses, values or people you've met
What the division does, and why it fits your strengths

questions.text: What questions would you like to ask us about the programme or the team?
covers: Specific questions about the work, training or team
A question that shows you've researched how the firm is organised
Nothing as general as 'What does Morgan Stanley do?'

tips: Know your CV well enough to talk through every line without reading it.
Have a reason for the industry, the firm and the division; Morgan Stanley's own interview guidance asks for all three.
Pick one or two areas of the markets you can discuss with knowledge and conviction, rather than trying to cover everything.
Learn how the firm is organised and its five core values, and ask specific questions rather than general ones.
If you don't know an answer, reason through it out loud; the firm's guidance says it's interested in how you work through a scenario.
For technology roles, practise coding and design questions while explaining your trade-offs as you go.
